summary: This Standards Track document defines COSE header parameters for signaling that a payload is the output of a hash function, so validation does not need the original payload. It also defines hints about the hashed content's format and where it can be found.

plainLanguage.summary: Sign a short fingerprint instead of the whole big thing, and add a note on where to find the original.

questions: what is a cose hash envelope
how to sign a hash with cose
subtitle: Sign a hash of a document instead of the document, and say where to find the original.

tldr.problem: Validating a COSE signature normally needs the full payload, which can be large and costly to move around, even though hashes are already widely used as identifiers for documents and software.
tldr.mechanism: A COSE_Sign1 carries the hash of the content as its payload, with new protected header parameters 258 (hash algorithm), 259 (content type of the hashed bytes) and 260 (location of the original).
tldr.outcome: Signature validation no longer needs the original content, and the hints let a verifier optionally fetch it and check that its digest matches the payload.

today: RFC 9995 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes, updates or is updated by it.

sections.title: Signing a Hash Instead of the Payload
sections.content:
Section 2 of RFC 9052 defines detached payloads for COSE, using nil as the payload. To verify a COSE_Sign or COSE_Mac, the recipient still needs access to the payload content.

Hashes are already used regularly as identifiers for payload data such as documents or software components. They are typically smaller than the data they represent, so they are simpler to transport, and using a hash as an identifier allows integrity checking. In some applications, such as remote signing, sending hashes instead of the original content reduces transmission time and costs.
sections.plainLanguage: A fingerprint is much smaller than the whole person. Sending just the fingerprint is faster, and it still proves who it belongs to.

sections.title: The Three New Header Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC specifies three new COSE header parameters. Label 258 (payload_hash_alg) names the hash algorithm used to produce the payload. Label 259 (payload_preimage_content_type) gives the content type of the bytes that were hashed (the preimage), either as a CoAP content-format number or as a media-type name optionally with parameters. Label 260 (payload_location) is an identifier that enables retrieval of the original resource.

The preimage is the set of input values to a function; a hash function applied to a message (the preimage) produces a digest value (the image).
sections.plainLanguage: There are three little labels on the signature: which fingerprint method was used, what kind of thing was fingerprinted, and where to find the real thing.

sections.title: The Hash Envelope Structure
sections.content:
A Hash Envelope is a COSE_Sign1 (CBOR tag 18) defined in CDDL. In the protected header, label 258 MUST be present, while labels 259 and 260 MAY be present and alg (1) names the signature algorithm. Labels 258, 259 and 260 MUST NOT appear in the unprotected header. Label 3 (content_type) MUST NOT appear in either header.

Label 3 is easily confused with 259. The difference is that content_type would describe the format of the payload itself, whereas payload_preimage_content_type describes the bytes that were hashed to produce the payload. When the content is a byte string, setting 259 to bstr makes clear that the preimage bytes were themselves a bstr, not the digest.

Hash output is small, so the payload is typically inline, but it can also be detached like in any other COSE message.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say which labels must be on the signature and which are forbidden. One label is easy to mix up with another, so the RFC explains how they differ.

sections.title: An SBOM Example
sections.content:
The informative example signs a System Package Data Exchange (SPDX) software bill of materials in JSON. The protected header uses ES384 (-35) as signature algorithm, sha256 (-16) as hash algorithm (258), the media type application/spdx+json (259) and a URL where the full JSON is available (260). The payload is the SHA-256 digest of manifest.spdx.json.

The resulting signature is computed over the protected header and the payload, so it protects the hash algorithm, content type and location of the associated resource, along with the hash.
sections.plainLanguage: The example signs the fingerprint of a parts list for a piece of software. The signature also covers the note saying what kind of file it is and where to download it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The hash and signature algorithm combination is RECOMMENDED to be at least as strong as the payload hash algorithm. For example, a payload produced with SHA-256 and signed with ECDSA should use at least P-256 and SHA-256. A pre-hash algorithm MUST be registered in the IANA COSE Algorithms registry and be distinguishable from non-pre-hash variants.

Only COSE_Sign/COSE_Sign1 and COSE_Mac/COSE_Mac0 are in scope. COSE_Encrypt and COSE_Encrypt0 are out of scope because there is no known use case at publication time; a future extension would need to settle whether the hash is applied before or after encryption and address privacy.

If a payload location is given, a verifier can choose to fetch the content and confirm its digest matches the payload. Verifiers without internet access that obtain the preimage by other means cannot perform that check.
sections.plainLanguage: The signing method should be at least as strong as the fingerprint method, or the chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Checking is optional: you can download the original and make sure its fingerprint matches.
